title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
1. Sviluppare un sistema nervoso



Il sistema nervoso emerge attraverso una sequenza coordinata di:

cambiamenti di forma
movimenti cellulari
segnali tra tessuti
acquisizione di identità regionali




Idea guida
Lo sviluppo non consiste nel semplice ingrandimento di una struttura: costruisce progressivamente differenze tra cellule e regioni.


Per la psicologia, comprendere questi passaggi aiuta a collegare organizzazione cerebrale, plasticità e vincoli dello sviluppo.

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
2. Foglietti embrionali ed ectoderma



Durante le prime fasi embrionali si distinguono tre foglietti:

ectoderma
mesoderma
endoderma



Il tessuto nervoso deriva da una porzione specializzata dell’ectoderma.



Immagine necessaria: schema dei tre foglietti embrionali con evidenza dell’ectoderma neurale
File proposto: images/nsdev_germ_layers.png

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
3. Neurulazione



La neurulazione trasforma una regione piatta dell’ectoderma in una struttura tubulare.

compare la placca neurale
i margini si sollevano
la regione centrale si incurva
le pieghe si avvicinano e si fondono




Immagine necessaria: sequenza schematica della neurulazione
File proposto: images/nsdev_neurulation.png

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
4. Placca, doccia e tubo neurale



Placca neurale
Ispessimento dell’ectoderma destinato a formare gran parte del sistema nervoso centrale.


Doccia neurale
Depressione mediana delimitata dalle pieghe neurali.



Tubo neurale
Struttura chiusa da cui si svilupperanno encefalo e midollo spinale.


Ai margini della placca si forma anche la cresta neurale, che seguirà un percorso distinto.

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
5. Timeline: giorno 18 e giorno 21



Intorno al giorno 18

la placca neurale è riconoscibile
inizia il rimodellamento dell’ectoderma

Si definisce progressivamente la linea mediana.



Intorno al giorno 21

la doccia neurale è evidente
le pieghe neurali si avvicinano

La formazione del tubo è in corso.



Immagine necessaria: confronto tra embrione al giorno 18 e al giorno 21
File proposto: images/nsdev_timeline_day18_day21.png


Le date servono come orientamento: i cambiamenti sono continui e parzialmente sovrapposti, non passaggi istantanei.

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
6. Chiusura del tubo neurale



La fusione non avviene simultaneamente lungo tutto l’embrione:

inizia in una regione intermedia
procede verso le estremità
lascia temporaneamente aperti i neuropori



La corretta chiusura separa il tubo neurale dall’ectoderma superficiale.



Immagine necessaria: progressione della chiusura del tubo neurale
File proposto: images/nsdev_neural_tube_closure.png

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
7. Cresta neurale e principali derivati



Le cellule della cresta neurale originano ai margini del tubo, si separano dal neuroepitelio e migrano in diverse regioni, dove assumono destini differenti.



Tra i principali derivati:

gangli sensitivi e autonomici
cellule di Schwann
melanociti
midollare del surrene
componenti craniofacciali



Immagine necessaria: vie migratorie e derivati della cresta neurale
File proposto: images/nsdev_neural_crest_derivatives.png

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
8. Induzione neurale



L’induzione neurale è il processo con cui segnali provenienti da tessuti vicini orientano una parte dell’ectoderma verso un destino neurale.


La posizione di una cellula determina quali segnali riceve, ma la risposta dipende anche dal suo stato interno.



Immagine necessaria: interazione tra tessuto induttore ed ectoderma competente
File proposto: images/nsdev_neural_induction.png

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
9. Spemann e Mangold: l’esperimento



Procedura

prelievo del labbro dorsale da una gastrula donatrice
trapianto nella regione ventrale di un embrione ospite
osservazione dello sviluppo successivo



Il trapianto induce la formazione di un secondo asse embrionale.



Immagine necessaria: schema del trapianto di Spemann e Mangold
File proposto: images/nsdev_spemann_mangold.png



Sottolineare che il tessuto trapiantato non costruisce da solo il secondo embrione: organizza anche cellule dell’ospite.

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
10. L’organizzatore di Spemann



Il tessuto trapiantato viene definito organizzatore perché può:

modificare il destino dei tessuti vicini
indurre strutture neurali
contribuire all’organizzazione degli assi corporei




Che cosa dimostra?
Lo sviluppo dipende da interazioni tra gruppi cellulari, non soltanto da istruzioni autonome già presenti in ogni cellula.


“Organizzare” non significa fornire un progetto completo: significa creare condizioni e segnali che coordinano risposte diverse.

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
11. Evidenze sperimentali in vitro



In coltura è possibile:

isolare porzioni di ectoderma
controllare i tessuti con cui interagiscono
modificare i segnali presenti
osservare l’acquisizione di caratteristiche neurali




Il confronto tra condizioni sperimentali mostra che l’identità neurale può essere influenzata dall’ambiente cellulare.


Limite
Una coltura semplifica il sistema: chiarisce relazioni causali, ma non riproduce l’intero contesto embrionale.



Collegare l’esperimento in vitro al trapianto: il primo isola variabili, il secondo conserva meglio l’organizzazione dell’embrione.

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
12. Regionalizzazione del tubo neurale



Il tubo neurale inizialmente continuo acquisisce identità differenti lungo due assi:

anteroposteriore
dorsoventrale



Le regioni diventano progressivamente diverse per struttura, tipi cellulari e connessioni future.



Immagine necessaria: tubo neurale con assi anteroposteriore e dorsoventrale
File proposto: images/nsdev_neural_tube_axes.png

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
13. Asse dorsoventrale e morfogeni



Segnali provenienti dalle regioni dorsali e ventrali formano distribuzioni graduate.
Questi segnali agiscono come morfogeni: cellule esposte a condizioni diverse possono acquisire identità diverse.



La risposta dipende da:

intensità del segnale
durata dell’esposizione
combinazione con altri segnali
competenza della cellula



Immagine necessaria: gradienti dorsoventrali nel tubo neurale
File proposto: images/nsdev_dorsoventral_morphogens.png

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
section: 14. Competenza cellulare e risposta ai segnali
text:
14. Competenza cellulare e risposta ai segnali



La competenza è la capacità di una cellula di rispondere a un determinato segnale.


Cellule diverse possono ricevere lo stesso segnale e produrre risposte differenti.



La risposta dipende da:

recettori disponibili
storia precedente della cellula
stato di differenziamento
momento dello sviluppo



Il significato di un segnale non è quindi fisso: dipende dal contesto.

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
15. Regionalizzazione anteroposteriore



Lungo l’asse anteroposteriore emergono grandi identità:

regioni encefaliche anteriori
mesencefalo
romboencefalo
midollo spinale




Immagine necessaria: identità regionali lungo l’asse anteroposteriore
File proposto: images/nsdev_anteroposterior_axis.png


La regionalizzazione è progressiva: domini inizialmente ampi vengono successivamente raffinati.

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
16. Acido retinoico e FGF



L’acido retinoico e i segnali FGF contribuiscono alla specificazione di identità posteriori del tessuto neurale.


Non agiscono come etichette isolate: il loro effetto dipende da quantità, tempo e contesto cellulare.



Principio generale
La posizione lungo un asse può essere tradotta in identità cellulare attraverso segnali distribuiti nello spazio e nel tempo.


Segnali simili possono sostenere funzioni diverse in fasi o regioni differenti.

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
17. Geni Hox e romboencefalo



I geni Hox contribuiscono a specificare l’identità anteroposteriore nel romboencefalo.

sono espressi in combinazioni regionali
aiutano a distinguere domini adiacenti
influenzano i destini neuronali




Immagine necessaria: romboencefalo segmentato con domini di espressione Hox
File proposto: images/nsdev_hox_hindbrain.png


Non vale una corrispondenza semplice “un gene = una struttura”: conta il profilo combinato.

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
18. Vescicole encefaliche



Vescicole primarie

prosencefalo
mesencefalo
romboencefalo



Queste espansioni rendono visibile la prima organizzazione macroscopica dell’encefalo.



Suddivisioni successive
Il prosencefalo dà origine a telencefalo e diencefalo; il mesencefalo mantiene la propria denominazione; il romboencefalo si suddivide in metencefalo e mielencefalo.


Immagine necessaria: passaggio dalle vescicole primarie alle suddivisioni successive
File proposto: images/nsdev_brain_vesicles.png

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
19. Regionalizzazione della neocorteccia



Le future aree corticali emergono dall’interazione tra:

differenze iniziali nei progenitori
segnali locali
maturazione delle connessioni
attività proveniente da altre regioni




Immagine necessaria: graduale comparsa delle aree nella neocorteccia
File proposto: images/nsdev_neocortex_regionalization.png


Le identità corticali iniziali non sono confini adulti già completi: vengono stabilizzate e raffinate durante lo sviluppo.

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
20. Protomap hypothesis



La protomap hypothesis propone che i progenitori corticali possiedano differenze regionali precoci.


Queste differenze forniscono una prima mappa delle future aree corticali prima della piena maturazione delle connessioni.



Predizione concettuale
Parte dell’identità di un’area dovrebbe essere riconoscibile anche prima dell’arrivo degli input sensoriali maturi.


Gli input successivi possono comunque modificare e affinare questa organizzazione iniziale.

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
21. Protocortex hypothesis e input talamici



La protocortex hypothesis attribuisce un ruolo centrale agli input talamici nel modellare l’identità funzionale delle aree corticali.


La corteccia iniziale viene considerata relativamente flessibile e progressivamente specializzata dalle connessioni in arrivo.



Immagine necessaria: confronto tra protomap e protocortex
File proposto: images/nsdev_cortical_hypotheses.png


Visione integrata
Fattori intrinseci e input talamici cooperano: le due ipotesi evidenziano pesi diversi, non processi necessariamente incompatibili.



Presentare protomap e protocortex come estremi interpretativi utili. La lettura contemporanea integra specificazione precoce e raffinamento dipendente dagli input.

title: Sviluppo embrionale del sistema nervoso
text:
22. Sintesi finale



Dal tessuto alla struttura:

l’ectoderma acquisisce identità neurale
la neurulazione costruisce tubo e cresta neurale
la chiusura modifica la geometria dell’embrione




Da struttura a organizzazione:
Induzione e competenza guidano le risposte; gli assi regionalizzano il tubo neurale; fattori intrinseci e input affinano la corteccia.


Messaggio chiave: lo sviluppo nervoso nasce dall’interazione continua tra posizione, segnali, storia cellulare e attività.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Building a nervous system



The nervous system emerges through a coordinated sequence of:

changes in tissue shape
cell movements
signals between tissues
acquisition of regional identities



Guiding idea
Development does more than enlarge a structure. It progressively creates differences between cells and regions.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Germ layers and ectoderm



Three germ layers become distinct during early embryonic development:

ectoderm
mesoderm
endoderm



Neural tissue develops from a specialized region of the ectoderm.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Neurulation



Neurulation transforms a flat region of ectoderm into a tubular structure.

the neural plate appears
its edges become elevated
the central region bends inward
the neural folds approach and fuse



Video

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
section: Neural plate, neural groove, and neural tube
text:
Neural plate, neural groove, and neural tube



Neural plate
A thickened region of ectoderm that will form much of the central nervous system.


Neural groove
A midline depression bordered by the neural folds.


Neural tube
The closed structure from which the brain and spinal cord will develop.


The neural crest gives rise to much of the peripheral nervous system, including sensory and autonomic neurons.


Video

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
5. Developmental timeline: day 18 and day 21



Around day 18

the neural plate is recognisable
remodelling of the ectoderm begins

The embryonic midline becomes progressively defined.



Around day 21

the neural groove is evident
the neural folds approach one another

Transformation towards a neural tube is under way.



Image needed: comparison of neural development around day 18 and day 21
Suggested file: images/nsdev_timeline_day18_day21.png


The dates provide orientation rather than sharp boundaries. These changes are continuous and partly overlap.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Neural tube closure



During closure:

opposing neural folds meet and fuse
surface ectoderm reconnects above the tube
the neural tube separates from the surface
the neuropores remain temporarily open



Disrupted closure can produce neural tube defects. The outcome depends on the affected region. Example: Spina Bifida

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
section: Neural crest and its main derivatives
text:
Neural crest and its main derivatives



Neural crest specification begins at the neural plate border, while the neural plate is still open.


After fusion, neural crest cells occupy the dorsal neural tube. They later delaminate and migrate to distant regions.



Major derivatives include:

sensory and autonomic ganglia
Schwann cells
melanocytes
the adrenal medulla
craniofacial components



Image needed: neural crest specification, delamination, and major derivatives
Suggested file: images/nsdev_neural_crest_derivatives.png

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text: Neural induction

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
The Spemann and Mangold experiment



Procedure

the dorsal lip was taken from a donor amphibian gastrula
it was transplanted into the ventral region of a host embryo
subsequent development was observed



The graft induced the formation of a secondary embryonic axis.





The graft did not build the entire secondary axis by itself. It also organized cells from the host embryo.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
10. The Spemann organiser



The transplanted tissue is called an organiser because it can:

alter the fate of nearby tissues
induce neural structures
contribute to the organisation of body axes




What does this show?
Development depends on interactions between groups of cells, not only on autonomous instructions within each cell.


To “organise” does not mean to provide a complete blueprint. It means creating signals and conditions that coordinate different responses.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
11. In vitro experimental evidence



In culture, researchers can:

isolate regions of ectoderm
control which tissues interact
vary the signals that are present
observe the acquisition of neural characteristics




Comparisons between experimental conditions show that the cellular environment can influence neural identity.


Limitation
A culture simplifies the system. It can clarify causal relationships but does not reproduce the complete embryonic context.



Connect the in vitro approach with transplantation: culture isolates selected variables, whereas transplantation preserves more of the embryo’s organisation.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
12. Regionalisation of the neural tube



The initially continuous neural tube acquires distinct identities along two axes:

anteroposterior
dorsoventral



Its regions progressively differ in structure, cell types, and future connections.



Image needed: neural tube showing its anteroposterior and dorsoventral axes
Suggested file: images/nsdev_neural_tube_axes.png

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
13. The dorsoventral axis and morphogens



Signals from dorsal and ventral regions form graded distributions.
These signals act as morphogens: cells exposed to different conditions can acquire different identities.



The response depends on:

signal strength
duration of exposure
combination with other signals
cellular competence



Image needed: dorsoventral signalling gradients in the neural tube
Suggested file: images/nsdev_dorsoventral_morphogens.png

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
section: 14. Cellular competence and response to signalling cues
text:
14. Cellular competence and response to signalling cues



Competence is a cell’s ability to respond to a particular signal.


Different cells can receive the same signal yet produce different responses.



The response depends on:

available receptors
the cell’s previous history
its state of differentiation
developmental timing



The meaning of a signal is therefore not fixed: it depends on context.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
15. Anteroposterior regionalisation



Broad identities emerge along the anteroposterior axis:

anterior brain regions
midbrain
hindbrain
spinal cord




Image needed: regional identities along the anteroposterior axis
Suggested file: images/nsdev_anteroposterior_axis.png


Regionalisation is progressive: initially broad domains are subsequently refined.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
16. Retinoic acid and FGF



Retinoic acid and FGF signalling contribute to the specification of posterior neural identities.


They do not act as isolated labels. Their effects depend on signal level, timing, and cellular context.



General principle
Position along an axis can be translated into cellular identity through signals distributed across space and time.


The same signalling system can support different functions in different regions or developmental phases.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
17. Hox genes and hindbrain organisation



Hox genes contribute to anteroposterior identity in the hindbrain.

they are expressed in regional combinations
they help distinguish adjacent domains
they influence neuronal fates




Image needed: segmented hindbrain with regional Hox expression
Suggested file: images/nsdev_hox_hindbrain.png


There is no simple correspondence between one gene and one structure. The combined expression profile matters.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Brain vesicles




Primary brain vesicles

forebrain
midbrain
hindbrain




Subdivisions
The forebrain forms the telencephalon and diencephalon.
The midbrain retains its name.
The hindbrain forms the metencephalon and myelencephalon.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
19. Neocortical regionalisation



Future cortical areas emerge through interactions between:

early differences among progenitor cells
local signalling cues
maturation of connections
activity arriving from other regions




Image needed: progressive emergence of areas in the developing neocortex
Suggested file: images/nsdev_neocortex_regionalisation.png


Early cortical identities are not complete adult boundaries. They are stabilised and refined during development.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
20. The protomap hypothesis



The protomap hypothesis proposes that cortical progenitor cells possess early regional differences.


These differences provide an initial map of future cortical areas before connections have fully matured.



Conceptual prediction
Some aspects of areal identity should be detectable before the arrival of mature sensory inputs.


Later inputs can nevertheless modify and refine this initial organisation.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
section: 21. The protocortex hypothesis and thalamic inputs
text:
21. The protocortex hypothesis and thalamic inputs



The protocortex hypothesis gives thalamic inputs a central role in shaping the functional identity of cortical areas.


The early cortex is regarded as relatively flexible and progressively specialised by incoming connections.



Image needed: comparison of the protomap and protocortex hypotheses
Suggested file: images/nsdev_cortical_hypotheses.png


Integrated view
Intrinsic factors and thalamic inputs cooperate. The two hypotheses emphasise different influences rather than necessarily incompatible processes.



Present the protomap and protocortex hypotheses as useful interpretative poles. Current accounts integrate early specification with input-dependent refinement.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Final summary



Key steps:

human embryology and model organisms provide complementary evidence
BMP inhibition supports neural induction
neurulation forms the neural tube and neural crest




Regional signals:

SHH patterns ventral neural tissue, while BMP and WNT pattern dorsal tissue
WNT, FGF, and retinoic acid contribute to anteroposterior identity



Key message: intrinsic patterning and external inputs work together throughout nervous system development.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Sources of evidence


To understand how the nervous system develops (and how brain activity gives rise to behaviour) we need a comparative perspective across species.


What can this comparison tell us?

Which mechanisms are conserved across species?
Which features are specific to humans?



Why study other animals?

Animal models allow us to manipulate genes, cells and circuits.
Many of these experiments would be impossible or unethical in humans.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Human neurulation timeline



Early neurulation

around day 18: the neural plate is visible
around days 20-22: neural-fold fusion begins




Neuropore closure

around day 25: the cranial neuropore closes
around days 27-28: the caudal neuropore closes

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Neural induction and BMP inhibition



BMP signaling promotes non-neural, epidermal development in the ectoderm.
Reducing BMP signaling allows competent ectoderm to adopt a neural fate.


The organizer releases BMP antagonists, including Noggin, Chordin and Follistatin. These signals support neural induction.





BMP inhibition is a central introductory model of neural induction. It does not represent every signal involved in neural development.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
The Spemann organizer



The transplanted tissue is called an organizer because it can:

alter the fate of nearby tissues
induce neural structures
contribute to the organization of body axes




What does this show?
Development depends on interactions between groups of cells, not only on autonomous instructions within each cell.


An organizer is not a complete blueprint. It creates signals and conditions that coordinate different cellular responses.



Even when the organizer is transplanted between different species, it can induce a secondary axis. For example, a chick organizer node transplanted into a zebrafish embryo recruits surrounding zebrafish cells to form a secondary axis.
The induced structures have the characteristics of the host species, not of the donor.
Organizer → instructive signals
Host cells → build the new tissues

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Animal-cap explant experiments



An animal cap is a small ectoderm explant removed from an amphibian blastula.
Researchers can culture it using in vitro Experimental techniques:

alone
with defined signaling conditions



The assay provides a simple test of how signals change ectodermal fate.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Regionalization of the neural tube



The initially continuous neural tube acquires distinct identities along two axes:

anteroposterior
dorsoventral



Its regions progressively differ in structure, cell types, and future connections.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Dorsoventral signals and morphogens



Ventral patterning: The notochord and floor plate provide SHH, a major ventral signal.
Dorsal patterning: The roof plate and nearby ectoderm provide BMP and WNT dorsal signals.


These signals form gradients. Cell identity depends on:

signal level
duration of exposure
interactions with other signals
cellular competence

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Cellular competence



Competence is a cell’s ability to respond to a particular signal.


Different cells can receive the same signal but produce different responses.



The response depends on:

available receptors
the cell’s previous history
its state of differentiation
developmental timing




A signal has no fixed meaning outside its cellular and developmental context.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Anteroposterior regionalization



Broad identities emerge along the anteroposterior axis:

anterior brain regions
midbrain
hindbrain
spinal cord



Regionalization is progressive. Broad early domains are later refined into more specific territories.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
WNT, FGF, and retinoic acid



WNT, FGF, and retinoic acid contribute to anteroposterior patterning.
Their level and timing help distinguish anterior from posterior neural identities.



Retinoic acid contributes to patterning anterior neural regions.
WNT and FGF support posterior neural character.



This model works well for the posterior neural tube and spinal cord. Patterning of the anterior nervous system is more complex and cannot be described by a single anteroposterior gradient alone.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Hox genes and hindbrain organization



The early hindbrain is organized into transient segments called rhombomeres.
Hox genes help assign anteroposterior identity to these regions.


Hox genes:

are expressed in regional combinations
help distinguish adjacent domains
influence neuronal identity




Image needed: hindbrain rhombomeres with regional Hox expression
Suggested file: images/nsdev_hox_hindbrain.png


There is no simple relationship between one Hox gene and one structure. The combined expression pattern matters.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Neocortical regionalization



Future cortical areas emerge through interactions between:

early differences among progenitor cells
local signaling cues
maturation of connections
activity arriving from other regions




Image needed: progressive emergence of areas in the developing neocortex
Suggested file: images/nsdev_neocortex_regionalization.png


Early cortical identities are not complete adult boundaries. They are stabilized and refined during development.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Classical hypotheses of cortical regionalization



Classical protomap hypothesis
Early regional differences in cortical progenitors provide an initial map of future cortical areas.


Classical protocortex hypothesis
The early cortex is relatively flexible. Thalamic inputs play a major role in shaping areal identity.


Integrated interpretation
Intrinsic patterning establishes early regional biases. Thalamic inputs and activity refine the developing cortical map.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text: Key concepts

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Sources of evidence



Human embryology
Mainly supports observation and description of developmental timing and anatomy.


Some experiments and developmental perturbations cannot be performed in humans for ethical and practical reasons.







Animal models
Amphibian, chick, and mouse models allow controlled manipulation of:

genes and tissues
signaling pathways
developmental conditions



Controlled perturbations make it possible to test causal hypotheses, rather than only describe development.
Many fundamental mechanisms are highly conserved across vertebrates. Species differences must still be considered when interpreting results.



Results from model organisms guide the interpretation of human development, but similarities should not be treated as complete equivalence.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
section: From one cell to many cell types
text:
From one cell to many cell types



Everything starts with a single cell: the fertilized egg, or zygote.

After fertilization, the zygote begins to divide repeatedly.
These first divisions produce cells that are different from most cells in the adult body. Stem cells differ in their developmental potential, that is, in how many different cell types they can generate.

Stem cells are not all the same. Their potential changes during development:
totipotent → pluripotent → multipotent → specialized cells




Totipotent cells: can generate all tissues
Pluripotent cells: can generate almost every cell type of the body
Multipotent cells: can generate several related cell types within a tissue
Oligopotent cells: can generate only a few closely related cell types
Unipotent cells: can generate only one specialized cell type



Differentiation: the process by which stem cells become specialized into specific cell types.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Dorsoventral signals and morphogens
Dorsoventral gradients contribute to the identity of neural progenitor cells.

SHH is highest ventrally, whereas BMP/WNT signals are stronger dorsally.
Cells sense the local concentration of these morphogens.
The gradient therefore acts as a positional map: it provides information about where a cell is located along the dorsoventral axis.
Different levels of morphogen exposure activate different intracellular signaling pathways and patterns of gene expression.
These molecular programs progressively specify different progenitor domains and neuronal identities.


A morphogen does not simply tell a cell what to become. Its concentration provides information about where the cell is, and the cell translates this positional information into a specific developmental fate.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Dorsoventral signals and morphogens 2



Dorsoventral gradients contribute to the identity of neural progenitor cells.

SHH is highest ventrally, whereas BMP/WNT signals are stronger dorsally.
Cells sense the local concentration of these morphogens.
The gradient acts as a positional map: it provides information about where a cell is located along the dorsoventral axis.
Different levels of morphogen exposure activate different intracellular signaling pathways and patterns of gene expression that progressively specify different progenitor domains and neuronal identities.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Ventral patterning: Sonic Hedgehog



SHH forms a ventral-to-dorsal concentration gradient in the developing neural tube.

Different SHH levels specify different ventral progenitor domains.
SHH binds PTCH, relieving its inhibition of SMO.
This activates GLI-dependent gene expression and promotes specific neuronal identities.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Dorsal patterning: BMP signaling


BMPs are produced dorsally and form a gradient opposite to SHH.


Different BMP levels contribute to the specification of dorsal progenitor domains.
BMP activates its receptors and the SMAD1/5–SMAD4 pathway.
Activated SMADs regulate gene expression and promote dorsal neuronal identities.




BMPs from the RP specify dorsal progenitors that become commissural interneurons.
BMP signaling also direct them to their ventral migration and axon guidance.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
section: Hox genes: from gradients to discrete regions
text:
Hox genes: from gradients to discrete regions



Morphogen gradients provide continuous positional information, but the nervous system must eventually be organized into distinct regions.
One example is the developing hindbrain, which is divided into transient segments called rhombomeres.


Rhombomeres are transient developmental structures.
They do not persist as separate units in the adult brain. During development, their cells are reorganized and contribute to the formation of the mature hindbrain, including structures and nuclei of the pons, medulla, cerebellar-related systems and cranial nerves.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
section: Hox genes: from gradients to discrete regions
text:
Hox genes: from gradients to discrete regions



Morphogen gradients provide continuous positional information, but the nervous system must eventually be organized into distinct regions.
One example is the developing hindbrain, which is divided into transient segments called rhombomeres.


Rhombomeres are transient developmental structures.
They do not persist as separate units in the adult brain. During development, their cells are reorganized and contribute to the formation of the mature hindbrain, including structures and nuclei of the pons, medulla, and cerebellar-related systems.


Hox genes translate positional information into regional identity.

different regions express different combinations of Hox genes
these combinations define distinct developmental domains
cells within each domain acquire related neuronal identities
these domains later contribute to the formation of distinct structures and nuclei




Image needed: hindbrain rhombomeres with regional Hox expression
Suggested file: images/nsdev_hox_hindbrain.png


The important principle is combinatorial coding:
continuous gradients → combinations of gene expression → discrete tissue identities
There is no simple correspondence between one Hox gene and one structure: it is the combination of expressed genes that matters.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
section: Hox genes: from gradients to discrete regions 2
text:
Hox genes: from gradients to discrete regions 2



Hox genes translate positional information into regional identity.



different regions express different combinations of Hox genes
these combinations define distinct developmental domains
cells within each domain acquire related neuronal identities
these domains later contribute to the formation of distinct structures and nuclei

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
section: From extracellular signals to brain regions
text:
From extracellular signals to brain regions

The Hox pattern in the hindbrain is just one example of a more general principle of nervous system development.
Gene expression is not established in isolation: it is continuously influenced by signals present in the extracellular environment.


Morphogens and other extracellular signals interact with receptors on the cell and activate intracellular molecular pathways.
These pathways modify the expression of transcription factors and other genes, initiating different developmental programs.


Through this process, initially similar cells acquire different identities and progressively organize into distinct domains, nuclei, and brain areas.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
section: Why is there no single “anterior morphogen”?
text:
Why is there no single “anterior morphogen”?



The anterior nervous system is much more structurally complex than the spinal cord. For this reason, anterior patterning depends on multiple local organizing centers, rather than on a single morphogen gradient.


Example: the isthmic organizer
The isthmus is located at the boundary between the developing midbrain and hindbrain.
It acts as an organizer by releasing signaling molecules, especially WNT1 and FGF8, that pattern the surrounding tissue and promote the development of the mesencephalon and metencephalon.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Regionalization of the neocortex

The developing neocortex initially appears relatively homogeneous, but it will become organized into many functionally distinct cortical areas.


Extracellular signals provide positional information. Different signaling centers produce gradients across the developing cortex:

FGFs particularly FGF8, from the anterior region
WNTs and BMPs from dorsocaudal regions

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
section: FGF8 helps organize the cortical map
text:
FGF8 helps organize the cortical map


Experimental manipulation of FGF8 changes the position of cortical areas:

increasing anterior FGF8 shifts cortical area boundaries posteriorly
adding an ectopic posterior source of FGF8 can generate a second, partially duplicated cortical map
even a second somatosensory area can appear

This shows that FGF8 is not simply correlated with cortical organization: it can instruct the position of cortical areas.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text:
Gene expression defines cortical regions


Morphogen gradients are translated into gradients of transcription factor expression.
Two important examples are Emx2 and Pax6, which are expressed in approximately opposing gradients across the developing neocortex.



Emx2 is higher toward caudomedial cortex.
Pax6 is higher toward rostrolateral cortex.
Different combinations and levels of these transcription factors give progenitor cells different regional identities.

title: Embryonic development of the nervous system
text: Self-check

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival



Once the nervous system has been regionalized, each region still has to be populated with the right number and the right types of cells.


This requires three closely connected processes:

neurogenesis: generation of neurons from neural progenitors
differentiation: acquisition of a specific neuronal identity
neuronal survival: selective maintenance or elimination of newly generated neurons



Video

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
section: From a progenitor to a neuronal population
text:
From a progenitor to a neuronal population

Neural development is not simply the production of neurons.
A progenitor population must be expanded, neurons must be generated at the correct time, acquire the correct identity, migrate to the correct place, and finally survive.


The final organization of the nervous system therefore depends on both constructive and selective processes.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Neurogenesis



Neurogenesis is the process by which neural progenitor cells generate neurons.
During prenatal development, enormous numbers of neurons are produced in a relatively short period of time.
Different brain regions and different neuronal populations are generated according to distinct developmental schedules.


During prenatal development, neurogenesis reaches an extraordinary rate.
At its peak, the human developing brain can generate approximately:
250k neurons per minute

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
section: Neural progenitors in the developing cortex
text:
Neural progenitors in the developing cortex



Early cortical progenitors are located close to the cerebral ventricles in the ventricular zone.
Many of these progenitors later acquire characteristics of radial glial cells.


Radial glial cells have two important developmental roles:

they act as neural progenitors
their long processes provide a scaffold for neuronal migration

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Expansion before differentiation

At the beginning of development, the priority is to increase the progenitor pool.
Later, progressively more divisions generate neurons and other neural cell types.




Proliferative divisions
Both daughter cells remain progenitors.
Result: expansion of the progenitor population.



Neurogenic divisions
One or both daughter cells leave the proliferative state and begin a neuronal developmental program.
Result: production of neurons.



Development therefore requires a balance between making more progenitors and using progenitors to make neurons.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Symmetric and asymmetric divisions



The outcome of a progenitor division can be different for the two daughter cells.


A symmetric proliferative division (or horizontal division) can generate:
progenitor: progenitor + progenitor


An asymmetric neurogenic division (or vertical division) can generate:
progenitor: progenitor + neuron

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Intermediate progenitors amplify neurogenesis






Not every neuron is generated directly by an apical progenitor.
Radial glial cells can also generate intermediate progenitor cells, which divide away from the ventricular surface.



Intermediate progenitors provide an additional amplification step. This strategy increases the number of neurons that can be produced from the original progenitor population.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Radial glia: progenitors and scaffolds



A newly generated cortical neuron must leave the proliferative zones and reach its final position in the cortical wall.


Many excitatory cortical neurons migrate along the long processes of radial glial cells.
The same cell type therefore participates in both:

generating neurons
guiding their migration

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
section: From the ventricular zone to the cortical plate
text:
From the ventricular zone to the cortical plate



The developing cortex is organized into transient developmental zones.
New neurons are generated near the ventricle and migrate toward the developing cortical plate.


As development proceeds:

progenitors remain concentrated in proliferative zones
newly generated neurons become postmitotic
neurons migrate outward
successive neuronal populations occupy different cortical positions

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
The cortex is built inside-out



Most cortical projection neurons are generated in a characteristic temporal sequence.
Earlier-born neurons settle in deeper cortical layers, whereas later-born neurons migrate past them and occupy progressively more superficial layers.


Simplified sequence:
early neurogenesis -> deep layers
late neurogenesis -> superficial layers

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Neuronal birthdate carries information

The time at which a progenitor undergoes its final mitosis is strongly related to the identity that its neuronal descendants can acquire.


Developmental time therefore acts as another source of information.
In the previous chapter, cells used spatial signals to understand where they were.
During neurogenesis, cells also change their developmental potential according to when they are generated.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Heterochronic transplantation




Heterochronic transplantation of cortical progenitors



Question

Does a cortical progenitor acquire its laminar identity only from the environment in which it is placed?



Approach

Progenitor cells are transplanted between hosts at different developmental ages.



Observation

The capacity of transplanted progenitors to adopt a new laminar fate depends on their developmental age and cell-cycle state.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
What heterochronic transplants show

Cortical progenitors do not remain equally flexible throughout development.
Their competence changes with developmental time.




Younger progenitors can still respond to environmental information and can, under appropriate conditions, adopt later neuronal fates.



As progenitors progress through development, their possible fates become progressively restricted.
After commitment and cell-cycle exit, neuronal identity becomes much less flexible.



A cell’s fate depends on both the environment it encounters and the developmental state of the cell when that signal is received.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Differentiation



Generating a neuron is only the beginning.
The newborn neuron must acquire a particular identity.


Differentiation includes the acquisition of properties such as:

patterns of gene expression
neuronal morphology
neurotransmitter phenotype
receptors and ion-channel expression
characteristic connectivity

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Intrinsic and extrinsic factors



Intrinsic factors
Information already present inside the cell can bias developmental fate.
Examples include:

transcription factors
asymmetric inheritance of cellular components
previous developmental history
current state of competence




Extrinsic factors
The cell also receives information from its environment.
Examples include:

secreted signaling molecules
signals from neighboring cells
extracellular matrix
target-derived factors




Neuronal identity emerges from the interaction between intrinsic state and extracellular signals.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Notch-Delta: lateral inhibition



Neighboring progenitor cells can influence whether they adopt a neuronal or support cell fate through Notch-Delta signaling. This process is called lateral inhibition and generates salt and pepper patterns.


A small initial difference between neighboring cells can be amplified:

a cell with stronger Delta activity (proneural) is driven toward a neuronal fate
Delta activates Notch in neighboring cells
Notch suppresses the proneural program in those cells (they remain in a progenitor/non-neuronal fate)

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Numb and asymmetric fate



Cell division can distribute molecules unequally between daughter cells.
One example is Numb, which can antagonize Notch signaling.


If the two daughter cells inherit different amounts of fate-regulating molecules, they can respond differently even though they originated from the same progenitor.


Asymmetric inheritance therefore provides one mechanism through which cell division can create different developmental trajectories.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
section: Transcription factors can constrain fate and migration
text:
Transcription factors can constrain fate and migration



Intrinsic developmental programs can control not only neuronal identity, but also the ability of neurons to reach the correct region.


An example is provided by Dlx1/Dlx2, transcription factors involved in the development of forebrain GABAergic interneurons.
Disrupting this program strongly alters the normal migration of interneuron precursors toward the neocortex.


Disruption of the Dlx developmental program reduce the number and function of cortical interneurons. This produces less inhibitory control of cortical circuits: In Dlx1 mutant mice, interneuron loss produces spontaneous generalized epileptic activity.




Dlx1/Dlx2-expressing interneuron progenitors are generated in the ganglionic eminences of the ventral telencephalon, adjacent to the developing striatum.
From there, they migrate tangentially into the developing cerebral cortex, where they differentiate into cortical GABAergic interneurons.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
section: The environment also instructs cell fate
text:
The environment also instructs cell fate



The fate of a developing cell is not determined only by where it was born.
Cells encounter new extracellular environments as they migrate.


These environments contain different:

signaling molecules
neighboring cell types
extracellular matrix components
target tissues



A migrating precursor can therefore receive new developmental instructions along its path.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
section: Neural crest: one population, many outcomes
text:
Neural crest: one population, many outcomes



Neural crest cells provide a clear example of multipotent progenitors whose fate depends strongly on the signals encountered during migration.


Neural crest derivatives include, among others:

sensory neurons
autonomic neurons
enteric neurons
Schwann cells
melanocytes

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Cell fate is an interaction

There is rarely a single factor that completely determines what a neural progenitor will become.


A useful way to think about differentiation is:
cell fate = intrinsic state + extracellular signals + developmental time + competence


The same extracellular signal can produce different outcomes in different cells because each cell has a different history, expresses different receptors, and activates different gene-regulatory programs.


Developmental signals provide information, but the cell must be competent to interpret it.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Neuronal survival



Neurogenesis produces more neurons than will ultimately be retained in many developing neuronal populations.


Becoming a neuron therefore does not guarantee becoming part of the mature nervous system.
Newly generated neurons must also pass through a period of selective survival.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Development includes programmed cell death

Programmed cell death is a normal component of nervous system development.
It is not the consequence of developmental failure.




Constructive processes

proliferation
neurogenesis
migration
differentiation
growth




Regressive processes

programmed cell death
elimination of transient cells
elimination of inappropriate projections
later elimination of synapses and branches




The mature nervous system emerges through a balance between production and selective elimination.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Apoptosis is not necrosis



Apoptosis
A regulated form of cell death.
Typical features include:

cell shrinkage
chromatin condensation
fragmentation into apoptotic bodies
removal by phagocytic cells
little inflammatory response




Necrosis
Usually follows severe cellular injury.
Typical features include:

cell swelling
membrane disruption
release of intracellular contents
inflammatory response

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
section: Apoptosis is an active molecular program
text:
Apoptosis is an active molecular program



Developmental apoptosis is an active biological program controlled by intracellular molecular pathways.


Examples of important regulators include:

BCL-2 family proteins that can promote survival
BAX and related proteins that promote apoptosis
caspases that execute the cell-death program



Cell survival therefore depends on the balance between pro-survival and pro-apoptotic signals.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Why eliminate neurons during development?



Programmed cell death can contribute to several developmental functions.


It can help:

match the size of interconnected neuronal populations
remove cells with inappropriate identities or connections
eliminate cells that served only a transient developmental function
refine developing structures




One of the most important principles of developmental neuronal survival is that neurons interact with the tissues they innervate.


Many developing neuronal populations initially contain more neurons than their targets can support.
Neurons that successfully interact with appropriate targets receive survival signals.
Neurons that do not receive sufficient support activate the apoptotic program.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Target tissues regulate neuronal survival

This mechanism helps match the number of neurons to the size and requirements of the target tissue.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Hamburger and Levi-Montalcini



Experiments in chick embryos by Viktor Hamburger and Rita Levi-Montalcini showed that peripheral target tissues influence the survival of developing neurons.


Manipulating the developing limb changed the number of spinal motor neurons that survived:

removing target tissue increased neuronal loss
adding extra target tissue increased neuronal survival

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
The target-manipulation experiment


Changing the amount of target tissue



Manipulation

The amount of peripheral tissue available to developing neurons is experimentally reduced or increased.



Result

Less target tissue → more neuronal death
More target tissue → more neuronal survival



Interpretation

Targets provide a limited resource required for neuronal survival.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
The neurotrophic hypothesis



The classical neurotrophic hypothesis proposes that developing neurons compete for a limited amount of target-derived survival factors.


The logic is:

many neurons project toward a target
the target produces limited trophic support
neurons compete for access to this support
neurons obtaining sufficient support survive
neurons receiving insufficient support undergo apoptosis

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
NGF and neurotrophic factors



NGF (Nerve Growth Factor) provided a molecular mechanism for the idea that target tissues can support neuronal survival.


NGF is essential for the development and survival of particular populations of peripheral sensory and sympathetic neurons.
It is not a universal survival factor for every neuron.


Different neuronal populations depend on different members of the broader family of neurotrophic factors.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
section: Competition matches neurons to their targets
text:
Competition matches neurons to their targets

Neurotrophic competition provides a mechanism for matching the size of a neuronal population to the size of the tissue it innervates.




Small or reduced target
less trophic support -> stronger competition -> more neuronal death



Large or additional target
more trophic support -> weaker competition -> more neuronal survival

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
section: Survival signals control the apoptotic program
text:
Survival signals control the apoptotic program

This is another example of the general developmental principle introduced earlier:
extracellular signals regulate intracellular molecular programs and gene expression.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Constructive and regressive processes

The mature nervous system is not created by simply adding cells. It is produced by repeated cycles of generation, selection, and refinement.




Constructive

progenitor expansion
neurogenesis
migration
differentiation
neuronal growth




Regressive

programmed neuronal death
elimination of inappropriate cells
later pruning of axons and synapses

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
From cells to circuits

At this point development has generated neuronal populations with characteristic identities and has adjusted how many of those neurons survive.


The next problem is how these neurons become connected into functional circuits:

how axons find their targets
how synapses are formed
how connections are refined
how axons become myelinated



Neurogenesis creates the cells. The next stage of development must connect them.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text: Apoptosis is not necrosis2

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text: The target-manipulation experiment

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text: The target-manipulation experiment 2

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Neurotrophic factors



Neurotrophic factors are extracellular signals that promote the survival, growth and differentiation of specific neuronal populations.


NGF: Nerve Growth Factor
NGF is especially important for the survival and development of particular populations of peripheral sensory and sympathetic neurons.






BDNF: Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor
BDNF supports the survival and differentiation of several neuronal populations in both the peripheral and central nervous system.
It also has important roles later in development in:

dendritic and axonal growth
synapse formation
synaptic plasticity



Different neurons depend on different neurotrophic signals.
NGF, BDNF, NT-3, and NT-4 belong to the neurotrophin family and act through specific Trk receptors.

title: Neurogenesis, differentiation and neuronal survival
text:
Competition for Survival



Neurotrophic competition provides a mechanism for matching the size of a neuronal population to the size of the tissue it innervates.


Small or reduced target
less trophic support -> stronger competition -> more neuronal death


Large or additional target
more trophic support -> weaker competition -> more neuronal survival



Target-derived trophic factors do not simply “feed” neurons.
They activate receptors and intracellular pathways that influence the balance between survival and apoptosis.


The extracellular environment can therefore regulate whether the intrinsic cell-death machinery is:
inhibited → neuron survives
or
activated → neuron undergoes apoptosis
